records.Entity / project type: decentralized reward-sharing pool protocol / public beta
records.Concise description: A 2026 public-beta Bitcoin reward-sharing system that lets miners keep local block-template construction while coordinating direct coinbase payouts without a central pool wallet.
records.Deeper researched summary: GridPool’s current public beta uses high-difficulty proofs of work in a bounded unpaid work set to create payout snapshots. Miners can build their own transaction templates, while successful GridPool blocks pay participating addresses directly from the coinbase transaction. The project explicitly describes itself as beta, with mainnet soft launch and Testnet4 validation, and currently supports DATUM as a preferred sovereign path plus bridge and native Stratum V2 beta options.
records.Launch / history: Public beta and mainnet soft launch were active in 2026; the project’s repositories and site were being updated in July–August 2026.
records.Why it matters in the Bitcoin mining eco: It explores pool-layer decentralization beyond template choice alone by also reducing centralized reward custody/accounting, while openly accepting higher variance and beta-stage tradeoffs.
Important technical or cultural characte: Public beta — not mature production infrastructure
Proof-of-work-ranked payout set rather than identity voting
DATUM integration and native SV2 beta
records.Verification basis: Current first-party site and repositories verify a live public beta/mainnet soft launch, architecture, payout design, and protocol integrations.
Research notes / uncertainties: Lifecycle ACTIVE refers to active development/public beta, not mature or broadly deployed production status.
Claims about attack resistance and variance reduction are project-model claims and should be attributed rather than presented as universally proven.

records.Concise description: A major 2013–2016 mining pool remembered for briefly exceeding or approaching half of observed Bitcoin network hashrate in 2014.
records.Deeper researched summary: GHash.IO became the focal point of Bitcoin mining-centralization concerns after measurements in June 2014 showed the pool coordinating more than half of recent network hashing over a short period. That did not mean the operator permanently owned that hashrate: independent miners could redirect their machines. The episode nevertheless demonstrated how concentrated pool coordination can create censorship, reorganization, and governance concerns even without changing Bitcoin’s consensus rules.
records.Launch / history: Operated during the 2013–2016 ASIC-mining era; its 2014 concentration episode became a major decentralization warning case.
records.Why it matters in the Bitcoin mining eco: It is the clearest historical case study for why pool concentration matters even when hashing hardware is independently owned.
Important technical or cultural characte: Short-lived majority/near-majority observed pool share in 2014
Pool concentration distinct from ownership of underlying machines
Inactive as a Bitcoin pool today

Corroborating sources.label: Federal Register discussion of GHash.IO concentration
Federal Reserve Bank of New York — Bitcoin mining concentration discussion

records.Verification basis: Government and central-bank research sources corroborate the 2014 concentration episode and historical significance; no current operation is represented.
Research notes / uncertainties: Historical estimates differ by measurement window; public copy should say 'briefly exceeded/approached 50% over short windows' rather than assert a permanent majority.
Do not imply GHash.IO owned all participating mining hardware.

records.Concise description: An influential early Bitcoin mining pool operated by Eleuthria from 2011 until its June 2015 shutdown.
records.Deeper researched summary: BTC Guild was a major shared pool through the GPU/FPGA and early ASIC eras and supported both pay-per-share and proportional/PPLNS-style pool accounting during its life. Operator communications document its closure on June 30, 2015 amid rising operational and regulatory concerns. It helps explain the transition from early community pools toward professionalized industrial pool infrastructure.
records.Launch / history: Opened in 2011 and shut down on June 30, 2015.
records.Why it matters in the Bitcoin mining eco: It was one of the dominant early pools and provides historical context for payout-model evolution, pool centralization concerns, and the operational burden of running a large pool.
Important technical or cultural characte: PPS and share-based payout models over its history
records.Verification basis: Operator communications and historical documentation verify its 2011–2015 operation and closure.
Research notes / uncertainties: Specific fee schedules changed over time and should not be presented as one timeless BTC Guild configuration.

records.Concise description: Luke Dashjr’s early no-registration Bitcoin mining pool, launched in 2011 and influential in direct coinbase payouts and getblocktemplate-era pool infrastructure.
records.Deeper researched summary: Eligius let miners identify themselves with Bitcoin payout addresses rather than conventional accounts and became associated with CPPSRB payout accounting and direct generation-transaction payouts. Its software/infrastructure lineage also intersects with Eloipool and the development/reference implementation of getblocktemplate. OCEAN later described itself as continuing important parts of the Eligius philosophy, but the historical Eligius service is not modeled as a current pool.
records.Launch / history: Launched April 2011; the original Eligius pool is historical rather than a currently active service.
records.Why it matters in the Bitcoin mining eco: It connects early pool design, non-custodial/direct payout ideas, and the emergence of getblocktemplate-based mining infrastructure.
records.Verification basis: Historical documentation and primary BIP references support Eligius’s role and technical lineage, but archival first-party pool material is incomplete.
Research notes / uncertainties: Source confidence is MEDIUM because current first-party archives for the original pool are incomplete.
Do not collapse historical Eligius into OCEAN; model the relationship explicitly.
